title: Arranging Vincent Youmans's music for Fletcher Henderson
summary: Henderson asked him to arrange Great Day music for Youmans, who played songs and had Marian Harris sing them; Youmans loved the results.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Leiderkrantz -- we finished up there and then it was shortly after that, it seemed to me, we made a few there, but maybe quite some time before we went over to Columbia, and made all the records at Columbia, and I think -- then we began to get into the Old Gold Show -- oh, going out to the coast, like the first time, I was working here in the city and I got a call one day from Fletcher, you know, he wanted to know if I'd like to do some arrangements for Vincent Youmans. Well, he said, his band was playing at --- Well, yeah, sure, this was "Great Day." It didn't last very long.
But the music did.
Oh, the music was beautiful. I'm a great admirer of Youmans' music anyway, but they were doing it in Columbus Circle, there was a Columbus Circle Theatre.
Circle Theatre.
Yeah, is that still there?
No.
I thought so.
That's where the Coliseum is, where they have the shows, the trade boat shows and all that sort of thing. That's where that was. I remember the theatre. I used to go there.
But it was a jinxed theatre. They had a lot of things there, particularly at that time.
I guess that's the original -- that's
the site where Riesenweber's was, where the Original -- so.
I think it was.
That's the same place, where the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played.

Right. Anyway, so they said, he come on down to the theatre now, because he's here and I talked to him, and he said, 'You can talk to him.' I don't know what had happened, but he evidently couldn't get anybody to do something he wanted, so I went down to the theatre and stayed around awhile and listened --
(Recording interruption)
You say you went down to Youman's rehearsal and nothing ever happened --

Nothing was happened then and he said, 'I got a tune,' he says, and he says, 'I want to have somebody do it and I want you to come over to my office,' and he said, 'There's a girl over there, Marian Harris. She's going to sing in the show and I want you to hear her sing. And make an arrangement,' and fine. I went over there, it was on the 24th floor of some building I used to know, but I don't know it now, and she was in the office there lying down on the couch, she had just come in town and she was tired. He made all the explanations and so forth, and he sat down at the piano and played.
He used to play, he had very full piano and then he'd whistle the melody, and he played it over, whistled the melody,
and so forth and gave me a copy of the first verse, and then he had her sing it.

She sang it beautifully. The verse and the chorus and then he had her do it again and do it again and he was a very understanding man, musician, music-wise anyway and he knew what arrangers -- you know, we got to get the idea. Of course, he wanted you to orchestrate pretty much what he had on the piano, the way he did it. So this was fine. So I took it home and week or so, whenever he wanted it, I had it done. He played it over and she sang -- I thought, 'Oh, God, he doesn't like it. I hope I did the right things,' I was having qualms about it. The phone rang and he gets on the phone and he says, 'Beautiful. Nice, kid, very good, very nice.' So I had done just pretty much what he wanted.

Fletcher liked it, and Hawkins, you know, he comes around later and he says, 'How come you didn't put a chorus in there for me? I wish I had.' Imagine, a real slow ballad -- well, anyway, that was good.

I had to get Whiteman's permission to do that which I got while he was out on the coast. And so you know, I figured it's another connection. It was good, nice experience and it was nice to work with somebody that likes your work. That sort of thing. Ideal conditions.
